source_text: His igitur absolutis vel breviter ostendam, quam iaceas in profundo ignorantiae, qui hactenus subtilissimus et acutissimus habebare. Dicis te naturae adscribere crimen, quod transit in sobolem, non tamen in nuptiis; sicut e regione, hominum naturae applicas, non flagitio. Et ideo fingis te quidem laudare connubium, ne aperte deprehendaris manichaeus; sed vituperas naturam, cui et malum inesse, et de qua propagari malum fateris. Numquam igitur audire potuisti disputationis regulas et sanissimae constituta rationis? In omnibus enim praedicamentis plus amplectuntur genera, quam species; inde autem etiam fiunt genera subalterna; plus autem species, quam atomi; suntque genera quibus species continentur, species autem speciales quibus individua concluduntur. Minorum ergo quassatio, superiora non quatit; superiora vero casibus suis omnia, quae complectebantur, involvunt. Verbi gratia, ani mal genus est: sed latitudine suae significationis diversas species comprehendit, scilicet hominis, equi, bovis, etc. Si ergo pereat una species, genus illud non sentit exitium; fac enim ut de rebus boum natura deficiat; genus nimirum interemptum non est, aliorum animalium permanente natura. At contra, si hoc quod est animal, auferatur de rebus; omnes sine dubio species, quae hoc genere concludebantur, intereunt; nulla enim remanebit species animantis, animali penitus interempto. Ea ergo quae superiora sunt, eventus suos atque merita speciebus, quas amplectuntur, impertiunt; non tamen recurrit, ut specierum suarum quasi necessitudinum quarumdam varietatibus permutentur. Utque ad causam referatur exemplum; naturae humanae generalitas institutionum infra se locatarum genus quoddam est; haec velut species habet, in situ, in membris, in ordinibus, in motibus, vel aliis id genus. Qualitatem ergo suam omnibus suppositis speciebus impertit; non tamen obnoxiaretur sui, ut minorum a se rerum periculis misceatur. Si ergo natura vituperetur, et obnoxia diabolo reaque credatur, coniugium quoque quod sub illa est, et fecunditas, et substantia tota damnabitur. Non potest ergo laudari connubium, quod fit secundum naturam, si natura ipsa reprehenditur. Commoriatur necesse est radici suae germinum succisorum venustas; et ut rem ipsam planius eloquar, non potest dici bonum negotium nuptiarum, si commixtio naturalis arguitur; quoniam quod depretiatur in genere, cui indivisibiliter adhaeret, in specie nequit honorari. Porro cum mala voluntas instrumentis naturalibus ad flagitia utitur, vis illa voluptatis et seminis, quae numquam pro coeuntium voluntate variatur, nullam patitur criminis societatem; sed materiam Deo praestat operanti, flagitiumque adulterantis solummodo arguit meritum, non naturae. Cum igitur de naturalibus disputaremus, perobtunse naturam reprobans connubia laudasti; cum irrefutabiliter constet genus speciebus suis participare, quidquid exceperit; et ideo aut usus, quem naturalem Apostolus dicit, bonus legitimusque censebitur, et erunt honesta coniugia, nullumque erit naturale peccatum; aut si creditur natura esse diabolica, ut sit originale peccatum, connubii quoque usus damnabilis pronuntiabitur. Et non quidem sobrie, ex aperto tamen Manichaeorum dogma suscipitur; quod quoniam funestum est, nec apud illos quidquam est aut veritatis, aut honestatis, aut fidei; apud nullos autem alios opinio potest naturalis esse peccati; ut nos catholicos, ita vos constat esse Manichaeos.
pass_a_gloss: These things therefore having been finished I will show even briefly how you lie in a depth of ignorance, you who thus far were held most subtle and most acute. You say you ascribe to nature a charge which passes into offspring, not nevertheless in marriages; as from the opposite side you apply humans to nature, not to outrage. And therefore you feign indeed that you praise wedlock, lest you be openly caught a Manichaean; but you blame nature, in which you confess both that evil is, and from which evil is propagated. Could you therefore never hear the rules of disputation and the constitutions of most healthy reason? For in all predicaments genera embrace more than species; from there however even subaltern genera are made; but species more than atoms; and there are genera by which species are contained, but special species by which individuals are enclosed. The shaking of lesser things therefore does not shake the higher; but the higher by their falls wrap all things which they were embracing. For example, animal is a genus: but by the breadth of its signification it comprehends diverse species, namely of human, of horse, of ox, etc. If therefore one species perish, that genus does not feel destruction; for make that the nature of oxen fail from things; the genus indeed has not been killed, the nature of other animals remaining. But on the contrary, if this which is animal is taken away from things; all the species without doubt which were enclosed by this genus perish; for no species of a living being will remain, the animal thoroughly killed. Those things therefore which are higher impart their events and deserts to the species which they embrace; yet it does not run back that they are changed by the varieties of their species as of certain kinships. And that the example may be referred to the cause; the generality of human nature is a certain genus of institutions placed below it; this has as it were species, in situation, in members, in orders, in motions, or others of that kind. It therefore imparts its quality to all the species placed under; yet it would not be made liable of itself, that it be mixed with the dangers of lesser things from itself. If therefore nature is blamed, and believed liable to the devil and guilty, marriage also which is under it, and fertility, and the whole substance will be condemned. Wedlock therefore cannot be praised, which is done according to nature, if nature itself is blamed. The beauty of cut germs must necessarily die with its root; and that I may utter the thing itself more plainly, the business of marriages cannot be called good, if a natural mingling is accused; because what is depreciated in the genus, to which it clings indivisibly, cannot be honored in the species. Further when an evil will uses natural instruments for outrages, that force of pleasure and of seed, which is never varied according to the will of those coupling, suffers no society of a charge; but it furnishes matter to God working, and the outrage of the adulterer accuses only desert, not nature. When therefore we were disputing about natural things, most bluntly blaming nature you praised marriages; when it irrefutably stands that a genus shares with its species whatever it has received; and therefore either the use which the Apostle calls natural will be judged good and legitimate, and marriages will be honorable, and there will be no natural sin; or if nature is believed to be diabolical, so that there may be original sin, the use of wedlock also will be pronounced damnable. And not indeed soberly, yet from the open the dogma of the Manichaeans is taken up; which since it is deadly, and among them there is nothing of truth, or of honorableness, or of faith; but among no others can the opinion of a natural sin be; as we are catholics, so you stand as Manichaeans.

pass_b_english: With these matters resolved, I will briefly show how deeply you lie in ignorance, although until now you were considered most subtle and acute. You say you attribute to nature, not marriage, the crime that passes to offspring, just as, on the other side, you attribute human beings to nature, not to a shameful act. You therefore pretend to praise marriage, to avoid being openly detected as a Manichaean, while criticizing nature, in which you confess evil exists and from which evil is propagated. Could you never hear the rules of argument and the principles of thoroughly sound reason? In every category, genera encompass more than species; subordinate genera also arise in this way. Species encompass more than individuals. Genera contain species, and the lowest species contain individuals. Shaking the lower things, then, does not shake the higher; but the higher things, by their own collapse, carry down everything they encompassed.

For example, ‘animal’ is a genus. In the breadth of its meaning it includes different species, such as human being, horse, ox, and others. If one species perishes, the genus does not suffer destruction. Suppose the nature of oxen disappears from existence: the genus is certainly not destroyed, since the nature of other animals remains. Conversely, if what ‘animal’ means is removed from existence, every species included under that genus undoubtedly perishes. No species of animate creature will remain once animal life is entirely destroyed. The higher things therefore share their fortunes and characteristics with the species they encompass. The reverse does not occur: the higher are not altered by the variations of their species as though by binding relationships.

To apply the example to the case: human nature in its generality is a kind of genus for the arrangements situated within it. It has, as it were, species in bodily position, organs, orders, movements, and other such things. It therefore shares its quality with all its subordinate species, but does not bind itself so as to share the risks of things lower than itself. If nature, then, is condemned and believed guilty and subject to the devil, marriage beneath it, fertility, and the whole substance will also be condemned. Marriage, which follows nature, cannot therefore be praised if nature itself is criticized. The beauty of severed shoots must die together with its root. To put the thing more plainly: the business of marriage cannot be called good if natural union is accused, since what is devalued in the genus to which it inseparably belongs cannot be honored in the species.

But when an evil will uses natural instruments for shameful acts, that power of pleasure and seed—which never varies according to the partners’ will—shares no part in the crime. It supplies material to God as he works, and the shameful act condemns only the adulterer’s deserving conduct, not nature’s. Since we were discussing natural things, your condemnation of nature alongside praise of marriage was exceedingly dull-witted. It is irrefutably established that a genus shares whatever it receives with its species. Therefore either the use the apostle calls natural will be judged good and legitimate, marriages will be honorable, and there will be no natural sin; or, if nature is believed diabolical so that original sin can exist, marital intercourse too will be declared condemnable. This is to embrace the Manichaeans’ doctrine, not soberly, but openly. Since that doctrine is deadly, and they possess nothing of truth, honor, or faith, while the theory of natural sin can belong to no others, it is established that we are catholics and you Manichaeans (compare Romans 1:27) (Romans 1:27).

choices.why: Julian names the opinion of original evil (mali originalis) as what Rom 5:12's 'one man' crushed; keep his phrase, not a later original-sin system.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)

choices.why: Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
